identity.title: Activation Oracles: Training and Evaluating LLMs as General-Purpose Activation Explainers

problem.claim: The paper investigates whether LLMs can serve as general-purpose natural-language explainers of LLM activations.

gap.claim: Prior LatentQA training and evaluation focused on narrow task settings, leaving generalist and far-out-of-distribution capability less examined.

contributions.claim: Evaluates LatentQA-trained Activation Oracles in far-out-of-distribution settings and studies how performance scales with training-data diversity.
Reports that Activation Oracles can recover fine-tuned information absent from input text, despite not being trained on activations from fine-tuned models.
Reports that adding classification and self-supervised context-prediction datasets produces consistent further improvements over narrowly trained models.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish their work by adopting a generalist perspective on LatentQA-trained activation explainers.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that their best Activation Oracles match or exceed white-box baselines on all four evaluated downstream tasks and exceed the best overall baseline on three of four.
The authors report recovery of fine-tuned biographical knowledge or malign propensities that do not appear in the input text, without training on fine-tuned-model activations.
The authors report that even narrowly trained models generalize well, with further consistent gains from additional diverse datasets.

narrative_sequence.summary: LLM activations are difficult to interpret, and existing methods are complex and specialized.
LatentQA simplifies interpretation by letting LLMs answer natural-language questions about activations, but prior work used narrow training and evaluation settings.
The paper adopts a generalist perspective and evaluates Activation Oracles under far-out-of-distribution conditions while varying training-data diversity.
The authors report recovery of hidden fine-tuned information, strong narrow-training generalization, and improvements from diversified training.

Across four downstream tasks, the best models reportedly match or exceed white-box baselines and beat the best overall baseline on three; the results suggest diversified natural-language-query training builds verbalization capability.

source_observation.claim: The abstract pairs a general capability claim with far-out-of-distribution evaluation, training-diversity scaling, and comparisons across four downstream tasks.

lessons.interpretation: A broad capability claim is made more inspectable by varying distribution and training diversity and by anchoring it to multiple task-level comparisons.
lessons.application: When presenting a general-purpose method, organize evaluation around distribution shift, controlled diversity changes, and a compact set of comparative downstream tasks.
lessons.exception: This structure may be unsuitable when the method is explicitly designed for one narrowly defined task or when comparable baselines are unavailable.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the four downstream tasks, dataset sizes or composition, model architectures, numerical performance, or details of the out-of-distribution settings.
The reported gains and baseline comparisons lack uncertainty estimates and experimental conditions in the supplied material.
